newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish pound claws back 2 pfennigs after battering.
newsitem.headline: Irish pound claws back 2 pfennigs after battering.

text.p: The Irish pound clawed back two pfennigs on Thursday after the previous day's battering which knocked it more than four pfennigs lower, but analysts said that while the short-term selling may be over, the currency's longer-term direction will be downwards.

The punt was knocked more than four pfennigs lower on Wednesday as the conviction that the punt/mark rate will have to fall ahead of the onset of a single currency caused another bout of heavy selling.
The Irish currency's decline attracted a few buyers, however, fuelling modest gains in morning trade on Thursday.
"We have opened this morning at very attractive levels to buy, particularly against sterling," one dealer said.

"As a result there is very little downside to the punt this morning. If the selling of the Irish pound of yesterday is exhausted then we are likely to see corporate interest in the Irish pound today."
By 1045 GMT the punt had recovered to 2.5735 marks from 2.5566 marks late on Wednesday. It was at 0.9280 stg versus 0.9180 and $1.5205 versus $1.5110.
Colin Hunt, economist at Bank of Ireland Group Treasury, said the punt was unlikely to fall below 2.55 marks in the short term.

"There is a near-term floor for the currency at 2.55 marks, although I would imagine that we will see further selling during the day," he said. "But for the moment I expect 2.55 to represent the floor."
Analysts said the long-term position of the punt was still precarious.

"I don't think the pressure on the punt will go away," Riada Stockbrokers chief economist Dan McLaughlin said. "The fundamental problem is still there -- the perception is that at the start of 1999 the authorities want it at its central rate of 2.41."

The punt charged to the top of the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) grid in 1996, spurred by a resurgent sterling, and has remained there ever since, at times more than 10 percent above its central ERM rate of 2.41 marks.

But as the conviction has grown that ERM central rates will be the eventual conversion rates for EMU and that Ireland will be part of the single currency, the punt's position has looked increasingly precarious.

Dealers said Wednesday's tumble was prompted partly by comments from Goldman Sachs. The investment bank recommended selling punts and buying the Finnish markka, pointing out that if the punt was not revalued it would drop towards its central rate.

Market talk that a more detailed report on the issue, due shortly from Goldman Sachs economist Martin Brookes, would be particularly bearish on the punt was the catalyst for much of Wednesday's selling, dealers said.
